quote: the dominant consensus in modern decision theory is that one should two-box
content: There was no consensus. In the 2009 PhilPapers survey, 31% of respondents accepted or leaned toward two-boxing and 21% toward one-boxing, with the rest undecided or otherwise (Bourget & Chalmers 2014). In 2020 the split was about 39% to 31% (Bourget & Chalmers 2023). A plurality is not a consensus, and one-boxing had distinguished defenders among evidential decision theorists. Casting the author's view as a lonely dissent from consensus serves the book's story about academia's inadequacy.

As stated, no decision theory can meet this. For any decision procedure, one can describe a predictor that rewards agents who don't use it; Omega could just as easily fill the box for causal decision theorists and leave it empty for everyone else. So "win" must be restricted to "fair" problems, in which rewards depend only on the agent's choices, and Yudkowsky & Soares's later paper on functional decision theory does exactly that (Yudkowsky & Soares 2017). Everything then depends on which problems count as fair. Newcomb's Problem, where the reward depends on a prediction of the agent's disposition, is precisely the contested case. The slogan relocates the dispute; it doesn't settle it.

quote: Rachel has a perfectly good answer to the “Why ain’t you rich?” question.
content: The essay engages Joyce but not the paper that named the argument. Lewis (1981), "Why Ain'cha Rich?", replied that the Newcomb predictor rewards irrationality. One-boxers are rich because they were predicted to be irrational, and a problem built to pay for a disposition can't show that the disposition is rational. One can reject Lewis's reply. But the essay repeatedly describes the causal decision theorist as defining winning "as conformance to a particular ritual," without meeting the argument that Newcomb's rewards are not a fair test of choices.

quote: This is a sufficient condition to imply that my utility function is unbounded.
content: It is not. Suppose utility is bounded: every finite life is worth at most 1, and living forever is worth 2. Then an 80% chance of living forever is worth at least 1.6 in expectation, which beats an 80.0001% chance of any finite life, worth at most about 0.8. The stated preference holds for every N under a bounded utility function. It shows only that living forever is valued above the limit of ever-longer finite lives. McGee (1999)'s argument for bounded utility is untouched by the example offered against it, and outcomes that last forever raise problems for expected utility that the essay doesn't consider.

quote: It is, I would say, a general principle of rationality—indeed, part of how I define rationality—that you never end up envying someone else’s mere choices.
content: Defining rationality so that the conclusion follows is not an argument for the conclusion. There are also well-known cases where envying a choice you can't rationally make is the right attitude. In Kavka (1983)'s toxin puzzle, you are paid tonight for intending to drink a mildly unpleasant toxin tomorrow. Once you are paid you have no reason to drink it, so you can't sincerely form the intention, and you rightly envy someone who can. Whether the rational response is to become such a person or to accept a predictable loss is the substance of the Newcomb debate. "Just do the act you envy" assumes an answer.

quote: I’ve now written a book-length exposition of a decision theory that dominates causal decision theory
content: "Dominates" is a claim, not a result. Timeless Decision Theory was never peer-reviewed. Its successor, functional decision theory, reached a philosophy journal only in a limited form (Levinstein & Soares 2020). It has been criticized for giving unclear or counterintuitive verdicts where it is unclear what counts as "the same algorithm," including by philosophers sympathetic to the project (Wolfgang Schwarz's 2018 referee report, published on his blog; William MacAskill's 2019 critique). A theory that one-boxes has its own costs. "CDT loses, the new theory wins" is its author's assessment, not the field's.

quote: start by looking at the agents who leave with a lot of money, develop a theory of which agents tend to leave with the most money
content: Judging decision procedures by who leaves a particular problem with the most money confuses good decisions with good outcomes. Lottery winners leave with a lot of money, and so do people a predictor happens to favor. Decision theory evaluates choices given the information and options available precisely because outcomes also reflect luck and the design of the problem. "Pay attention to the money" is a sound heuristic when problems are fair. In problems designed to reward dispositions, it is the question at issue, not an answer to it.
